lessons.title: Reading the news like an analyst
lessons.summary: You will be able to turn any business headline into a 2-minute analysis and an interview-ready sentence: the facts, why now, winners and losers, second-order effects, the numbers and the market reaction.

sections.h: Why reading a lot is not enough

sections.body:
For every story you really want to understand, answer these 7 questions in this order. At first it takes you 5 minutes; after a few weeks 2 are enough.

| # | Question | What you are looking for | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **What happened?** | Who, what, how much. Rewrite the fact without adjectives, with the key number | 15 s |
| 2 | **Why now?** | The trigger: a data release, a deadline, a political decision, a shock, a change in the cycle | 15 s |
| 3 | **Who wins, who loses?** | Sectors, countries, currencies, consumers, debtors and creditors. Every story shifts value from someone to someone else | 20 s |
| 4 | **And then?** (second order) | How competitors, regulators, central banks and customers will react over the next 6-18 months | 20 s |
| 5 | **Which numbers do I check?** | The base for comparison: expectations, history, share of the total, order of magnitude | 20 s |
| 6 | **How did the market price it?** | Was it expected? What did equities, bond yields, currencies, credit spreads and commodities do | 15 s |
| 7 | **How do I say it in one sentence?** | Fact + why it matters + what I would watch next | 15 s |

**The heart of the method is questions 3 and 4.** Anyone can repeat the headline; few candidates can say who gains from it and what will happen next. That is where you already sound like an analyst.

A tip for question 3: **follow the money along the value chain**. If the price of an input rises, whoever sells it earns more and whoever buys it sees margins fall, unless it can pass the increase on to the end customer. Always ask who has **pricing power**, that is, the ability to raise prices without losing customers.

sections.h: Expected versus unexpected: the rule that explains markets
sections.body:
Prices already reflect expectations. That is why **a market reacts to the surprise, not to the news**. Inflation at 3% can push stock markets up if the consensus expected 3.4%, and push them down if it expected 2.7%.

**Where to find expectations without a terminal:**
- for macro data, articles almost always quote the economists' **consensus** ('economists polled had expected...');
- for central banks, rate futures show the probability of a cut or a hike ('markets had priced in...');
- for listed companies, results and **guidance** are compared with analysts' estimates: guidance often matters more than the quarter just ended.

**Three expressions to know:**
- **Priced in**: the news was expected, so the effect on prices happened before the announcement.
- **Buy the rumour, sell the news**: a price rises in anticipation of good news and falls when it arrives, because the surprise is over.
- **Risk-on / risk-off**: with optimism, equities, high yield and emerging-market currencies usually rise; with fear, high-quality government bonds, the dollar, the Swiss franc, the yen and gold rise.

The most widely used relationship of all: **a bond's price and yield move in opposite directions**. 'Yields rose' means bonds lost value. Among the benchmark maturities, the 2-year yield is the most sensitive to expectations for policy rates; the 10-year also reflects growth, expected inflation and the borrower's risk.

These rules hold **all else being equal**: they are the starting point, not the conclusion. The added value lies in understanding when, this time, the rule does not hold.

| If this happens... | Usually wins | Usually loses |
|---|---|---|
| Rates higher than expected | The country's currency, savers, banks in the short term (net interest margin) | Bonds already issued, real estate, highly indebted companies, growth stocks, LBOs |
| Sharp rise in oil | Energy-exporting countries and companies, currencies of producer countries | Airlines, chemicals, transport, consumers, net importing countries |
| Strong dollar | Non-US exporters selling in dollars, dollar-based investors | Emerging markets with dollar debt, US multinationals (foreign revenues are worth less in dollars), commodity prices, quoted in dollars |
| Import tariffs | Protected domestic producers, in the short term | Importers, consumers in the country imposing the tariff, targeted exporters, sectors exposed to retaliation |
| Recession fears | High-quality government bonds, defensive sectors (consumer staples, healthcare, utilities) | Cyclical sectors (industrials, autos, luxury), high yield, small caps |
| Inflation higher than expected | Those with strong pricing power or indexed revenues, inflation-linked bonds | Fixed-rate bonds, those whose costs rise faster than their selling prices |

**The bridge to your job.** For a bank analyst, every macro story reaches the desk through four channels:
- **cost of financing**: rates and credit spreads decide how much a debt-financed acquisition costs;
- **valuation multiples**: for the same growth, higher rates mean lower multiples;
- **board confidence**: with uncertainty, deals get postponed;
- **market windows**: IPOs, bond issues and leveraged finance open and close with volatility.

Closing a macro argument with 'and for M&A activity this means...' sets you apart from those who stop at the economics.

sections.h: The numbers: five checks before you believe them
sections.body:
A headline uses adjectives; you must use numbers with their base. Before repeating a figure, run these checks:

1. **Compared with what?** With expectations, with the same period last year, with the historical average. A 'record' in nominal terms is often not one in real terms, that is, net of inflation.
2. **Per cent or percentage points?** If a rate goes from 2% to 3%, it has risen by 1 percentage point (100 basis points) but by 50% in relative terms. 25 bp = 0.25 percentage points.
3. **Over what period?** Month on month, year on year, annualised quarter. US GDP is reported as an **annualised** quarterly change; Eurozone and UK GDP as a **non-annualised** quarterly change. A European +0.5% quarter is equivalent to roughly +2% annualised, US-style.
4. **How much does it weigh on the total?** A 500 million fine makes headlines, but for a group with 50 billion of revenue it is 1%. Always scale it to revenue, EBITDA, market capitalisation or GDP.
5. **Is it a base effect?** 40% growth after a year of collapse may only bring the level back to where it was before.

**Mental maths that always comes in handy:**
- 25 bp more on 1 billion of floating-rate debt = 2.5 million more interest per year;
- rule of 72: growth of 7% a year doubles a value in about 10 years (72 / 7);
- inflation of 3% a year halves purchasing power in about 24 years (72 / 3).

sections.h: From the story to the interview sentence
sections.body:
Question 7 is the one you will actually use. The most effective format is **What, So what, Now what**, in 30-45 seconds:
- **What**: the fact with a number ('The central bank raised rates by 50 bp, twice what the market expected').
- **So what**: why it matters and for whom ('That tightens financing conditions, which hurts leveraged borrowers and real estate').
- **Now what**: what you will watch next and which fact would disprove your view ('If the next inflation print does not slow, the market will price further hikes').

**How to prepare:**
- Always have **3 stories** ready: one macro (rates, inflation, currencies), one sector or deal story, one geopolitical or trade story. Follow them for weeks, not for a day.
- For each story write a sheet with the 7 answers, the sentence in English and the most likely follow-up question ('What would change your mind?').
- Check against **primary sources**: central bank statements, statistics offices, press releases and presentations of listed companies.
- Know the calendar: the Fed, the ECB and the Bank of England set rates about 8 times a year; the US monthly jobs report usually comes out on the first Friday of the month.
- Every Sunday reread your sheets: what actually happened compared with what you had predicted? It is the fastest way to train your judgement.

**A confidentiality rule:** in an interview never reveal non-public information, not even vaguely. If you are asked about a deal you worked on, stick to what is already public or describe it anonymously (type of deal, your role, what you learned), without names, numbers or details that make it recognisable. Anyone who leaks confidential details of their current employer is rejected, because the bank assumes they would do the same with its clients.

sections.h: The mistakes that make you sound junior
sections.body:
- **Repeating the headline without a 'so what'.** If your answer ends where the article ended, you have added nothing.
- **A single cause for a market move.** Markets move for several reasons at once; better to say 'one of the drivers was...'.
- **Wrong numbers stated with confidence.** A correct order of magnitude ('around 2%') is better than an invented decimal.
- **Taking political positions.** Analyse the economic effects of a decision, do not judge whoever made it. 'Who wins and who loses' is neutral; 'it is a stupid policy' is not.
- **Confusing short and long term.** A tariff can help a domestic producer for a year and hurt it afterwards, if its imported inputs cost more or retaliation follows.
- **Forgetting the other side.** Every cost for someone is revenue for someone else: if you cannot find who wins, you have not yet understood the story.
- **Stories that are too old or too niche.** Choose stories from the last few weeks that are big enough to interest whoever is listening.

examples.q: Headline: 'Central bank raises its policy rate by 50 basis points to 4.0%; markets had priced in 25 bp. The currency rises 1.2%, the 2-year government bond yield jumps 20 bp and the equity index falls 1.5%.' Analyse it with the 7-question method and give your 30-second take (What, So what, Now what).
steps: What happened: a 50 bp hike against 25 expected. The surprise is 25 bp, and that is what moves prices, not the hike itself.
Why now: probably inflation is not falling fast enough, or the central bank wants to rebuild credibility. Check this in the statement and at the press conference.

Winners and losers: the currency, savers, banks in the short term and importers (stronger currency) win. Floating-rate mortgages, real estate, highly indebted companies and funds, growth stocks and exporters lose.
And then: weaker real estate, wider credit spreads, more expensive refinancing, LBOs harder to finance and therefore less sponsor M&A in the following months; the government's interest bill rises.
Numbers to check: the real rate (4.0% minus current inflation), how many more hikes the market now prices, the committee vote (unanimous or split), the consensus for the next inflation print.

How the market priced it: the 2-year yield rises 20 bp, so the market reads the move as a signal of tight policy in the future as well. Equities down and the currency up are consistent with a hawkish surprise.
examples.answer: 'The central bank hiked by 50 bp against 25 expected, a clear hawkish surprise; the move in the 2-year yield shows the market now expects rates to stay higher for longer, which raises financing costs for leveraged borrowers and should slow sponsor-led deal activity. The next inflation print is the key test.'

examples.q: Headline: 'A listed European industrial group agrees to buy a US rival for USD 12bn in cash, a 30% premium to the undisturbed share price. The acquirer's shares fall 7% (market capitalisation before the announcement: USD 30bn); the target's shares rise 26%.' What does the market reaction tell you?
steps: What happened: an all-cash cross-border acquisition at a 30% premium. The 12 billion includes the premium, so the target's market value was about 12 / 1.30 = 9.2 billion and the premium is worth about 2.8 billion.
Why now: the strategic logic is access to the US market, scale and cost synergies; the timing often depends on a favourable financing window or the fear that a competitor moves first.

Winners and losers: the target's shareholders win, and often so do the other possible targets in the sector, which rise because the market expects further consolidation. The acquirer loses, for now: 7% of 30 billion = about 2.1 billion of value destroyed, about three quarters of the premium.

And then: antitrust review in several jurisdictions with possible forced disposals, a bridge loan later refinanced with bonds (work for DCM and leveraged finance), the risk of a counterbid, competitors facing a bigger rival.

Numbers to check: implied EV/EBITDA against peers and precedent transactions, post-deal leverage (net debt / EBITDA), synergies net of integration costs compared with the 2.8 billion premium, accretion/dilution on EPS.

How the market priced it: the target's shares rise 26% against an offered premium of 30%, so the merger arbitrage spread is 1.30 / 1.26 - 1 = about 3%: the market expects the deal to close. The acquirer's fall says investors give little credit to the synergies or worry about the leverage.
examples.answer: 'Strategically logical, but the market thinks the buyer overpaid: it lost about USD 2bn of value, roughly three quarters of the USD 2.8bn premium, so investors give little credit to synergies. The 3% arbitrage spread says they expect the deal to close; antitrust and post-deal leverage are what I would watch.'

examples.q: Headline: 'Country A imposes a 25% tariff on imported cars; its largest trading partner, Country B, promises retaliation on A's agricultural exports.' Who wins, who loses, and what would you watch?
steps: What happened: a 25% tariff on imported cars. On a car imported at 30,000 dollars, that is 7,500 dollars to be split between the exporter (lower margin), the importer and the consumer (higher price). Who really pays depends on pricing power: this is the question of the economic incidence of the tariff (tax incidence).

Why now: protecting a sector with many jobs, gaining more bargaining power in a trade negotiation, the electoral cycle. Ask yourself whether it is a negotiating move, often temporary, or a structural one.

Winners and losers: in the short term A's carmakers win. B's exporters, A's consumers and A's farmers hit by retaliation lose. A's producers that use imported components also suffer, because car supply chains cross borders several times.

And then: production moved inside A to get around the tariff (tariff-jumping), trade flows diverted towards third countries, higher inflation in A, a weaker currency in B that partly offsets the tariff, a dispute at the WTO.
Numbers to check: the share of imports in A's car market, the weight of sales to A in the revenue of B's exporters, A's agricultural exports exposed to retaliation.

Market and history: B's car stocks and its currency usually fall, while A's producers rise only a little because they too have global supply chains. Precedents to cite: the US Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 triggered retaliation and contributed to the collapse of world trade in the early 1930s; the 1964 'chicken tax', a 25% US tariff on light commercial vehicles (pick-ups and vans) introduced as retaliation against French and West German tariffs on American chicken, has remained in force for decades.
examples.answer: 'Short term it protects A's carmakers, but the bill is paid by A's consumers and, through retaliation, by its farmers; the second-order risks are higher input costs for A's own producers and a tit-for-tat escalation. I would watch whether this is a negotiating tactic or permanent, and how much of the tariff exporters absorb in their margins.'

cheatsheet: 7 questions: what happened, why now, who wins and who loses, and then, which numbers, how the market priced it, the sentence.
The market reacts to the surprise relative to the consensus, not to the news itself.
Every story shifts value from someone to someone else: if you cannot find who wins, you have not yet understood the story.
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions; the 2-year reflects expectations for policy rates.
Percentage points are not per cent: from 2% to 3% = +100 bp, but +50% in relative terms.
US GDP: annualised quarterly; Eurozone and UK: non-annualised quarterly (roughly x4 to compare).
Always scale the number to a base: revenue, EBITDA, market capitalisation, GDP.
Bridge to banking: cost of financing, multiples, board confidence, market windows.
Interview sentence: What, So what, Now what, in 30-45 seconds.
Three stories always ready (macro, deal or sector, geopolitics) and never anything non-public.

lessons.title: The map of the world economy
lessons.summary: You will be able to place every story on the durable map of the global economy: who produces and exports what, why the dollar dominates, who sets the rules, where goods travel and how capital moves, with the right orders of magnitude.

sections.body:
Every economic story rests on a structure that changes slowly: who produces what, in which currency payments are made, who writes the rules, where ships pass, who lends to whom. If you have this structure in your head, a new story immediately hooks onto something you already know.

The map has **five layers**:
1. **The economic blocs** and what they export.
2. **Currencies**, and why the dollar is at the centre of everything.
3. **The institutions** that set the rules and lend in crises.
4. **Chokepoints**, the physical and non-physical bottlenecks of trade.
5. **Capital flows** between surplus and deficit countries.

**Rule on numbers:** here you will find only rounded, stable orders of magnitude, dated where necessary. In an interview a correct order of magnitude ('the US is roughly a quarter of world GDP') is worth more than a decimal that may already be out of date.

**The exercise that makes it stick:** every week pick a country and write 5 lines (what it exports, what it imports, exchange-rate regime, current account surplus or deficit, which chokepoint it depends on). Once a month redo the tables in this lesson from memory: what you cannot remember is what you need to revise.

sections.h: The orders of magnitude to keep in mind
sections.body:
| Measure | Order of magnitude | How to use it |
|---|---|---|
| World population | About 8 billion (threshold crossed in 2022) | India and China about 1.4 billion each, with India the more populous since 2023; EU about 450 million, US about 340 million (mid-2020s) |
| Nominal world GDP | Over 100 trillion dollars (mid-2020s) | US about a quarter; China and the EU about a sixth each: the three poles together make up about 60% |
| The other large economies | Germany, Japan, India, the UK, France, Italy: in the order of 2-5 trillion each (mid-2020s) | The ranking among them changes over the years: remember the band, not the position |
| World trade | Exports of goods and services equal to about 30% of world GDP | Over 80% of goods, by volume, travel by sea |
| Oil | World consumption around 100 million barrels a day | +10 dollars a barrel = about 1 billion dollars a day more paid by the world |
| Foreign exchange market | Several trillion dollars traded every day (BIS surveys of the 2020s: between about 7 and 10 trillion) | It is the largest market in the world by volume: that is why currencies are the first to react to macro surprises |
| Stock markets | The United States accounts for over 60% of the main global equity indices (mid-2020s) | That is why the US cycle dominates portfolios all over the world |

A trick to remember them: **8, 100, 100, 30, 80**. Eight billion people, over a hundred trillion of GDP, a hundred million barrels a day, trade around 30% of GDP, over 80% of goods by sea.

sections.h: The blocs and what they export
sections.body:
- **United States**: services (finance, software, intellectual property, entertainment), aircraft, soybeans and maize, energy: thanks to shale, in 2020 it became a net exporter of oil and petroleum products on an annual basis for the first time since records began (1949), and it is among the largest exporters of liquefied natural gas. A structural goods trade deficit for decades, financed by the rest of the world.
- **China**: large-scale manufacturing (machinery, electronics, steel, vehicles, batteries, solar panels). The world's largest exporter of goods since 2009, about 30% of world manufacturing output (mid-2020s). The largest importer of crude oil, iron ore and soybeans: every Chinese slowdown shows up immediately in commodity prices.
- **European Union**: a single market of about 450 million people, with trade policy run at EU level. Machinery, cars, chemicals and pharmaceuticals (Germany), aerospace and luxury (France), engineering, fashion and food (Italy). A net energy importer: oil and gas shocks hit growth and inflation at the same time.
- **Japan and South Korea**: cars, machinery, electronic components, steel, ships. They import much of their energy and almost all their oil and gas. Japan has been among the world's largest net creditors for decades: it was the very largest for over thirty years from 1991, before being overtaken by Germany in the end-2024 data.
- **Gulf countries** (Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait): oil and gas, with Qatar among the leading exporters of liquefied natural gas. Currencies largely pegged to the dollar and sovereign wealth funds that reinvest the proceeds around the world.
- **Russia**: oil, gas, wheat, fertilisers, metals. In 2022 it was hit by broad Western sanctions that redirected its energy flows towards Asia.
- **India**: IT and back-office services, generic drugs, refined petroleum products. A large importer of oil and gold; for years the world's largest recipient of remittances from emigrants.
- **Latin America**: Brazil (soybeans, iron ore, meat, coffee, sugar), Chile and Peru (copper), Mexico (manufacturing integrated with US supply chains).
- **Canada and Australia**: Canada exports oil (it is the largest supplier of crude to the US), gas, metals and potash; Australia iron ore, coal and liquefied natural gas, with China as its largest customer.
- **Africa**: oil, gas, gold, cobalt (the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines over 70% of it), cocoa (Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together over half of world supply). According to UN projections, by around 2050 about one in four people in the world will be African.

**The analyst's reading:** countries divide into **commodity exporters and commodity importers**. When commodity prices rise, income shifts from the latter to the former, and with it currencies, current accounts and public finances.

sections.h: The dollar: why everything goes through it
sections.body:
**The durable numbers (IMF and BIS data, mid-2020s):** the dollar accounts for more than half of the foreign exchange reserves reported by central banks, the euro about a fifth, all other currencies together the rest (the yen and sterling a few percentage points each, the yuan around 2%). In the foreign exchange market the dollar is on one side of almost 9 trades out of 10, and most commodities, starting with oil, are priced in dollars.

**Why the dollar in particular:**
- US Treasuries are the largest and most liquid government bond market in the world: anyone who needs to park hundreds of billions finds there the safest place and the easiest to liquidate;
- capital free to enter and leave, the rule of law, an independent central bank;
- **network effect**: if oil is paid for in dollars and debts are in dollars, it makes sense to hold reserves in dollars;
- banks all over the world lend and fund themselves in dollars (the eurodollar market): in a crisis everyone looks for dollars, and the Fed opened swap lines with other central banks both in the 2007-2009 financial crisis and in the 2020 pandemic.

**The story you need to be able to tell:**
- **1944, Bretton Woods**: fixed exchange rates against the dollar, convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce. The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are created.
- **1960s**: the French finance minister Valéry Giscard d'Estaing speaks of the 'exorbitant privilege' of the United States, which borrows in its own currency. The economist Robert Triffin describes the dilemma that bears his name: to supply the world with the dollars it needs, the US must run external deficits that in the long run undermine confidence in the dollar.
- **1971**: President Richard Nixon suspends the convertibility of the dollar into gold. From 1973 the main currencies float.
- **1999**: the euro is born (notes and coins from 2002), since then the second reserve currency.

**What it means for an analyst:** when the dollar strengthens, financial conditions tighten all over the world. Emerging markets with dollar debt pay more in local currency, oil costs more for those who pay for it in euros or yen, capital flows back to the US. That is why it is said that the Fed is, in effect, the world's central bank.

| Institution | Founded, headquarters | What it does | Why it matters to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Federal Reserve** | 1913, Washington | US central bank with a dual mandate: maximum employment and price stability. The FOMC sets rates at 8 meetings a year | Its rate is the world's benchmark price of money |
| **ECB** | 1998, Frankfurt | Central bank of the Eurozone; primary mandate price stability, inflation target of 2% over the medium term. Since 2014 it has directly supervised the area's large banks | Euro rates and spreads between member states' government bonds |
| **Bank of England** | 1694, London | Among the oldest central banks (the first is the Swedish Riksbank, 1668); the Monetary Policy Committee pursues a 2% inflation target set by the government | Sterling, gilts and the London market |
| **IMF** | 1944, Washington | Lends to countries in balance-of-payments crises in exchange for reforms (conditionality), monitors economies, publishes the World Economic Outlook in April and October | It is the emergency room for countries in currency crises |
| **World Bank** | 1944, Washington | Long-term loans and assistance for development and poverty reduction; its IFC arm finances the private sector | Infrastructure and development in emerging countries |
| **WTO** | 1995 (successor to the 1947 GATT), Geneva | Trade rules: most-favoured-nation clause (non-discrimination) and dispute settlement, whose appellate body has been paralysed for years since December 2019 because the United States blocked the appointment of new members | It is the legal framework for tariffs and retaliation |
| **BIS** | 1930, Basel | The central banks' bank; it hosts the Basel Committee, which writes banks' capital rules (Basel I in 1988, II in 2004, III from 2010, after the 2008 crisis) | Capital rules decide how much your bank can lend and to whom |
| **G7** | 1975 (Canada from 1976), no headquarters | Forum of the large advanced economies: US, Japan, Germany, UK, France, Italy, Canada, with the EU taking part | Coordination among advanced countries, sanctions |
| **G20** | 1999 (ministers), leaders' summits since 2008 | 19 countries plus the EU and, since 2023, the African Union; over 80% of world GDP | The forum that coordinated the global response to the 2008 crisis |
| **OPEC and OPEC+** | 1960 and 2016, Vienna | Cartel of oil producers led by Saudi Arabia; since 2016 the OPEC+ alliance has included other producers led by Russia. Together they pump over 40% of the world's crude (mid-2020s) and control most of the spare capacity. | Its production quotas move the oil price |

**How to tell them apart in one sentence:** the IMF is the **crisis doctor** (loans to countries in currency difficulty), the World Bank the **development financier** (long-term projects), the WTO the **trade referee**, the BIS the **central banks' club**. A detail that impresses: by a convention born after the war, from their founding until at least the mid-2020s the IMF has been led by a European and the World Bank by an American.

Much of seaborne trade passes through a few straits. When one closes or slows down, freight rates rise, deliveries are delayed and energy prices react within hours.

| Chokepoint | Where | What passes through | Remember |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strait of Hormuz** | Between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula | In normal times about a fifth of the oil consumed in the world (EIA data, 2024) and almost all of Qatar's liquefied natural gas | The most important energy chokepoint; few pipeline alternatives. |
| **Strait of Malacca** | Between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, with Singapore at the southern exit | The shortest route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific: energy and goods for China, Japan and Korea | Among the busiest straits in the world |
| **Suez Canal and Bab el-Mandeb** | Egypt; southern entrance to the Red Sea between Yemen and Djibouti | The main route between Asia and Europe | Opened in 1869, nationalised by Egypt in 1956 (Suez crisis); since the end of 2023 attacks on ships in the Red Sea have pushed many shipowners to go round the Cape of Good Hope |
| **Panama Canal** | Isthmus of Panama | Link between the Atlantic and the Pacific | Opened in 1914, handed over to Panama at the end of 1999; it uses fresh water from an artificial lake, so the 2023-2024 drought reduced transits |
| **Turkish Straits** (Bosphorus and Dardanelles) | Turkey | The only outlet from the Black Sea: grain, oil | Governed by the 1936 Montreux Convention |
| **Strait of Dover** | Between England and France | Access to the major ports of Northern Europe | Among the busiest shipping lanes in the world |

**The calculation you need to be able to do.** If an Asia-Europe voyage goes from about 30 to about 40 days because ships sail round the Cape of Good Hope, with the same number of ships the fleet's effective capacity falls by about a quarter (30 / 40 = 0.75), or about a third more ships are needed (40 / 30 = 1.33) for the same service. That is why a diversion pushes freight rates up far more than the fuel cost alone.

**Non-physical chokepoints** matter just as much:
- **concentrated production**: China refines about 90% of rare earths, the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines over 70% of cobalt;
- **submarine cables**, which carry almost all intercontinental data traffic;
- **the dollar payments system**, which runs through US correspondent banks and is the main instrument of financial sanctions.

**The identity to start from:** current account balance = national saving - investment. Those who save more than they invest (China, Germany, Japan, the Gulf countries, Switzerland, the Netherlands) run a surplus and **lend the difference to the rest of the world**. Those who consume and invest more than they save (the United States, the United Kingdom) run a deficit and **must attract capital**. The balance of payments always balances: a current account deficit is financed by a net capital inflow of the same amount.

**The channels, from the most stable to the most volatile:**
- **Foreign direct investment (FDI)**: factories, controlling acquisitions. Slow to enter and to exit.
- **Reserves and sovereign wealth funds**: surplus countries recycle their earnings into foreign assets, above all US Treasuries. Norway's sovereign wealth fund, fed by oil, is among the largest in the world; in the 1970s people spoke of petrodollar recycling.
- **Remittances** from emigrants: for many emerging markets they are worth more than foreign direct investment.
- **Portfolio investment and bank lending**: equities, bonds, cross-border loans, often in dollars. Liquid, they move with rates and sentiment.
- **Carry trade**: borrowing in a low-rate currency (historically the yen and the Swiss franc) to invest where yields are higher. When it unwinds quickly, the funding currencies jump and the financed assets fall.

**The trilemma (impossible trinity):** a country cannot have a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and an independent monetary policy all at once. It must give up one of the three.

| Choice | Gives up | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Free capital + own monetary policy | Fixed exchange rate: the currency floats | United States, United Kingdom, Japan |
| Free capital + fixed exchange rate | Own monetary policy | Hong Kong (pegged to the dollar since 1983), Denmark (pegged to the euro), Eurozone countries among themselves |
| Managed exchange rate + own monetary policy | Free capital movement | China, with capital controls |

**The cycle that repeats:** when US rates rise and the dollar strengthens, capital leaves emerging markets, especially those with external deficits and dollar debt. The 1982 Latin American debt crisis, the 1994 Mexican crisis, the 1997 Asian crisis and the 2013 taper tantrum follow this pattern, with differences.

**In an interview** the map gives you the structure for open questions such as 'What is the biggest risk to the global economy?': which layer is hit (energy, currencies, trade, capital), which countries and sectors are most exposed, which institution can react and with what tools.

examples.q: Oil rises by USD 10 a barrel and stays there for a year. Roughly how much more does the world spend on oil, in dollars and as a share of world GDP, and who wins and who loses?
steps: Volume: world consumption is around 100 million barrels a day.
Extra cost per day: 100 million x 10 dollars = 1 billion dollars. Over a year: about 365 billion.

Relative to world GDP (over 100 trillion): 365 / 100,000 = about 0.36%, a little less with GDP of 110-120 trillion (about 0.3%). It is not wealth that disappears: it is a transfer from net importers to net exporters.

Losers: the large net energy importers (Eurozone, Japan, Korea, India, China), their consumers and energy-intensive sectors. Winners: the Gulf, Russia, Norway, Canada. For the United States, a net exporter of oil and products, the overall effect is close to zero but it redistributes: consumers pay more for petrol, producers earn more.

Second order: higher headline inflation in importers and less room to cut rates, worse current accounts and pressure on their currencies; exporters build up surpluses and recycle them through sovereign wealth funds.
examples.answer: About 1 billion dollars a day, that is, about 365 billion a year: roughly 0.3-0.35% of world GDP, transferred from net energy importers to net exporters.

examples.q: The US dollar appreciates 10% against an emerging-market currency (from 20 to 22 local units per dollar) as US rates stay high. A company in that country earns in local currency but has USD 500m of dollar debt. What happens to it, and who else is exposed?
steps: Mechanical effect: the debt was worth 500 million x 20 = 10 billion in local currency and is now worth 500 million x 22 = 11 billion. It grows by 10% in local currency without a single new loan.
Watch the base: the dollar rises by 10%, but the local currency loses about 9.1% (1 - 20 / 22), not 10%.

Dollar interest also costs 10% more in local currency, while revenues stay in local currency: leverage (net debt / EBITDA) worsens and the risk of breaching covenants rises. This is currency mismatch.

Who else is exposed: emerging markets with current account deficits and a lot of dollar debt, importers of commodities paid for in dollars, US multinationals whose foreign revenues are worth less in dollars. Who benefits: exporters that sell in dollars and have costs in local currency.

Response of emerging-market central banks: raise rates or sell reserves to defend the currency, even when the domestic economy would not call for it. This is the channel through which Fed policy is transmitted to the rest of the world.
examples.answer: The debt rises from 10 to 11 billion in local currency (+10%) without new borrowing and leverage worsens; all dollar borrowers with revenues in another currency, emerging markets with external deficits and commodity importers are exposed.

examples.q: A small open economy pegs its currency to the US dollar and allows free capital movement. The Federal Reserve raises rates sharply and capital starts flowing out. What are the central bank's options, and what does history suggest?
steps: Trilemma: with a fixed exchange rate and free capital, the country has already given up its own monetary policy. Four options remain.
Raise rates in line with the Fed: this defends the exchange rate but slows the domestic economy, even if it is already weak. This is the Hong Kong route, pegged to the dollar since 1983.
Sell dollar reserves to buy its own currency: this works as long as reserves last. Markets look at how many months of imports they cover and how much short-term external debt they must back.
Introduce capital controls: free capital movement is given up, at a reputational cost with foreign investors. Malaysia did so in 1998, during the Asian crisis.

Abandon the peg and devalue: Thailand did so in July 1997, setting off the Asian crisis; the United Kingdom left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism on 16 September 1992, Black Wednesday. The opposite case, with capital flowing in: in January 2015 the Swiss National Bank unexpectedly abandoned the minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro.
Lesson: a peg is only as credible as the reserves that defend it and the willingness to tolerate high rates. When markets doubt both, a speculative attack accelerates the crisis.
examples.answer: Raise rates, use reserves, impose capital controls or devalue: with free capital it cannot hold a fixed exchange rate and an autonomous monetary policy together. Thailand in 1997 and the United Kingdom in 1992 show what happens when the peg can no longer be defended.

cheatsheet: Three poles: US about a quarter of world GDP, China and the EU about a sixth each (mid-2020s); together about 60%.
Guide numbers 8, 100, 100, 30, 80: billions of people, trillions of GDP, millions of barrels a day, trade as % of GDP, % of goods by sea.
Oil: +10 dollars a barrel = about 1 billion dollars a day, about 0.3-0.35% of world GDP over a year.
Dollar: over half of reserves, on one side of almost 9 FX trades out of 10; euro about a fifth of reserves.
Strong dollar = tighter financial conditions worldwide and emerging markets with dollar debt under pressure.
Dates: Bretton Woods 1944, end of gold convertibility 1971, floating exchange rates from 1973, euro 1999.
IMF the crisis doctor, World Bank development, WTO the trade referee, BIS the central banks' bank and the Basel rules.
Chokepoints: Hormuz (in normal times about a fifth of the oil consumed in the world), Malacca, Suez and Bab el-Mandeb, Panama, the Turkish Straits, Dover.
Current account = saving - investment; a deficit is always financed by net capital inflows.
Trilemma: fixed exchange rate, free capital, autonomous monetary policy: at most two out of three.
